title: On‑Prem Kubernetes Provisioning Checklist & Terraform Playbook (iteration 1)
body:
Purpose:
This is a pragmatic, ops‑focused playbook for provisioning on‑prem Kubernetes clusters that we expect to run Redwood inference workloads. It captures a working checklist for both bare‑metal and vSphere environments, notes on the Terraform modules we iterate on, and a conservative upgrade plan for minor/major K8s releases.

Scope and assumptions:
- Target clusters: 3–20 nodes (initial), GPU + CPU nodes separated by node pools.
- Control plane: HA (3 masters) recommended for production; single control-plane for PoC only.
- CNI: Calico (policy + networking) by default; plan includes steps for switching to Cilium later.
- Provisioning options covered: PXE/iPXE bare metal + vSphere cloning/template flow.
- Kubernetes installation: kubeadm (preferred for reproducibility) with our preflight hooks; we can evaluate k0s or k3s for very small edge clusters later.
- Image registry: private registry (harbor or GCR/Artifact registry mirror) reachable from nodes.

Inventory checklist (before you start):
- IP ranges (control-plane, worker, serviceCIDR, podCIDR) documented in network spec.
- DNS entries or DNS delegation for kubernetes API VIP.
- NTP/chrony configured across nodes.
- Access to KMS for cluster secrets (optional for Private deployment).
- vSphere template with cloud-init for kubelet bootstrap OR PXE images (iso/iPXE) for bare metal.
- BMC/IPMI credentials for each bare-metal chassis.
- GPU firmware/driver compatibility matrix (NVIDIA driver + CUDA version).

High-level provisioning flow (common):
1) Prepare infra config in Terraform: networking, DNS records, load balancer (HAProxy/MetalLB for bare-metal or vSphere LB).
2) Provision compute resources (bare metal: orchestration via MAAS/ipmi -> ipxe; vSphere: clone from template via Terraform/vSphere provider).
3) Configure OS baseline: distro image (Ubuntu 22.04 LTS for now), disable swap, set sysctl, install container runtime (containerd), nvidia drivers on GPU nodes.
4) Bootstrap control plane(s) with kubeadm + external etcd or stacked HA as configured. Apply bootstrap manifests from our kustomize repo.
5) Join worker nodes, label GPU nodes, deploy device-plugin + GPU drivers.
6) Deploy CNI, ingress (Contour/Traefik), registry mirror, and RBAC policies.
7) Run smoke tests: nginx deployment, GPU scheduling test, kube-proxy check, basic e2e.
8) Snapshot cluster state and push terraform state to remote backend (S3/GCS) + lock.

Bare‑metal specifics (notes & gotchas):
- PXE chain: ipxe -> fetch a small cloud‑init tarball -> run cloud-init that pulls the bootstrap script. Keep scripts idempotent.
- IPMI quirks: some vendors return wrong power states; add small retry loops (3 attempts) in the provisioning script.
- MetalLB: use layer2 mode for smaller DCs; BGP for network teams who can announce prefixes.
- Disk partitioning: avoid destructive defaults; we prefer LVM on /var/lib/containerd for easier resize.
- GPU nodes: install NVIDIA driver from package repo but pin exact version in Terraform variable (driver_version).

vSphere specifics (notes & gotchas):
- Template customization: use cloud-init + guestinfo to pass bootstrap tokens. Test template on all target ESXi versions.
- vSphere provider: be explicit about folder/datacenter/resource pool to avoid surprises.
- Collect VM UUID mapping to node names; use that for inventory reconciliation.
- Datastore latency matters for kubelet stability; prefer local SSD or fast SAN for workloads with high IO.

Terraform module notes (current iteration):
- Module: infra/networking: inputs: api_vip, pod_cidr, service_cidr, dns_zone. Outputs: lb_ip, dns_names. Known issue: dns_zone optional flag sometimes creates duplicate records when team DNS and infra DNS overlap.
- Module: compute/baremetal: exposes ipmi_creds, provisioning_profile, node_mac_list. TODO: add idempotent tagging for nodes to avoid reprovisioning healthy nodes.
- Module: compute/vsphere: input template_name, power_on, clone_timeout. Make sure to set clone_timeout >= 900s for large templates.
- Module: k8s/bootstrap: wraps kubeadm config generation + prints join command as a file in /opt/bootstrap. We should add a flag to choose stacked vs external etcd.
- State management: remote S3 backend with locking (DynamoDB) for prod; local state for dev. Add automated plan + apply pipeline that requires manual approval for changes touching LB / control-plane.

Terraform gotchas to document for operators:
- Provider credential expiry: recommend using short‑lived service accounts and a refresh script that runs in CI.
- Race condition: multiple applies creating identical DNS records — serialize via state locks.
- Sensitive outputs: avoid printing kubeadm tokens in CI logs — write them only to secrets store.

Kubernetes bootstrap sequence (detailed):
- On control plane node 1: run kubeadm init --config /opt/kubeadm-config.yaml --upload-certs
- Apply network plugin manifest and wait until coredns + kube-proxy are ready.
- Join additional control plane nodes: kubeadm join ... --control-plane --certificate-key <file>
- Worker nodes: kubeadm join ... (use join tokens from secrets store or ephemeral certs)
- Post-join: label nodes (node-role.kubernetes.io/worker=), taint GPU nodes: nvidia.com/gpu.present=true

Upgrade plan (minor first, major with caution):
- Pre-upgrade: run cluster-health scripts; snapshot etcd; backup PVs for critical stateful apps.
- Staging cluster upgrade test: create an identical staging cluster from VM templates + terraform state and run upgrade.
- Minor upgrade (e.g., 1.26.x -> 1.26.y): cordon & drain nodes in rolling fashion, kubeadm upgrade apply on control-plane, then kubelet/kubeadm on workers. Monitor API server latency and control-plane pod restarts.
- Major upgrade (e.g., 1.25 -> 1.26): run deprecation checks, ensure runtime compatibility (containerd + CRI versions), upgrade kubeadm and kubelet binaries first, validate on staging. Consider creating a canary node-pool and migrating low-risk workloads first.
- Rollback: keep machine images for quick reprovision; restore etcd snapshot if control plane becomes unhealthy.

Operational playbook: quick commands & checks
- Check control-plane: kubectl get componentstatuses (deprecated) -> instead check kube-apiserver metrics and logs via kube-system pods.
- Node health: kubectl get nodes -o wide; describe node for kubelet errors.
- GPU plugin: kubectl get ds -n kube-system nvidia-device-plugin-daemonset; kubectl describe pod <device-plugin> for driver mismatch.
- Etcd: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status <snapshot> and etcdctl endpoint status — ensure certificate rotation scheduled.

Troubleshooting snippets (common incidents):
- Nodes failing to join: check time sync, swap disabled, CRI socket path, and kubelet version mismatch.
- API unreachable after HAProxy change: ensure healthcheck path is /healthz and cert SANs include VIP.
- GPU scheduling failing: confirm nvidia driver + nvidia-container-runtime installed, device-plugin logs show discovery.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Add automated e2e test harness for inference pipeline as smoke test (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/e2e-harness/pull/12).
- Formalize canary node-pool policies (size, traffic shift percentage).
- Document exact compatibility matrix for NVIDIA driver/CUDA/containerd for all supported GPUs.
- Add terraform variable to choose k8s distribution (kubeadm | k0s) and validate both paths.

Notes to self:
- Keep all bootstrap scripts idempotent and write logs to /var/log/infra-provisioning.log.
- Avoid using ephemeral tokens in CI logs — always write secrets to vault.

Appendix: quick references
- kubeadm config template path: /opt/kubeadm-config.yaml
- Terraform state: s3://redwood-terraform/private-deployments/<env>/state
- Contact oncall: #oncall-infra, pager duty: infra-oncall

End of playbook (iteration 1). This doc is intentionally practical and terse — expand into separate runbooks for bare-metal PXE flows and vSphere template grooming when we get to iteration 2.
